p1-saved-carts.reason: B gives engineering priorities and concrete acceptance tests and names who must decide each open item, which makes it closer to a buildable PRD. A is cleaner and more faithful on reminder emails (and its 30-day reasoning is useful), but its requirements are bare one-liners. Close call; both pass 6 of 7.
p1-saved-carts.assertion_notes: Assertion 4 is debatable for reminder emails: the notes do show a disagreement (loyalty wants them, PM says no), so B's 'open question' reading is defensible, though the PM's statement makes non-goal the more natural reading. Assertion 6 passes B only leniently: R7 has no real acceptance check. Assertion 3's 'no invented date' does not say whether a document date header counts; I treated it as not a project fact.

p2-bulk-export.reason: A is the fuller PRD: numbered, prioritised requirements with acceptance tests and every open item carrying positions and an owner. B is accurate and its rough Q1 feasibility arithmetic is the single most useful insight in either document, but as a requirements doc for engineering it is thin.
p2-bulk-export.assertion_notes: Assertion 4 is ambiguous for B: it introduces dates (2026-11-20, 2027-03-31) and week counts beyond the notes, but flags them as its own arithmetic to be confirmed; I passed it, a strict reader could fail it. That arithmetic is arguably a strength, so the assertion penalises useful analysis. Assertion 5 is met by A only loosely, since A also keeps the scheduled export as requirement R7.

Decision 3 'How is opt-in collected for clients who booked by phone and have no number on file?' is muddled: clients with no number cannot be texted regardless of opt-in; the real gap is opt-in collection for all existing clients.

p3-reminders.reason: Both are factually faithful and both pass every assertion; B is more usable because each requirement has a priority and a concrete test and the open items have suggested owners. A is tighter and has no invented requirement, but leaves eng to work out priority and done-ness.
p3-reminders.assertion_notes: Assertion 2 asks for a 'Must' requirement; A has no priority scheme at all, so I passed it on its 'not optional' wording - a strict reading would fail A. Assertion 6 is ambiguous about A's '$120 for 10,000 reminders' illustration (correct arithmetic, hypothetical volume). This packet has no assertion on priorities/acceptance checks, unlike the other two, so equal pass counts hide a real usability gap.
